source_evidence.observation: Machine epsilon is denoted epsilon, and stable multiplication satisfies ||C_comp-C|| <= mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| + O(epsilon^2), where mu(n)=O(n^c) is a low-degree polynomial. The paper permits changing norms at the cost of further dimension-dependent polynomial factors.

source_evidence.anchor: opening of Section 3, Logarithmically stable algorithms
source_evidence.observation: The section abandons strict backward stability and uses extra precision to attain approximately the forward accuracy of a backward-stable method. The precision increase is described as proportional to log n and the resulting cost increase as polylogarithmic.

Logarithmic stability means a relative error O(epsilon) kappa_f(x)^{chi(n)} + O(epsilon^2), where chi(n) is polynomial in log n. Matching backward-stable accuracy raises precision from b_bs to at most chi(n)b_bs+O(1) bits and bit complexity by at most a quadratic factor in chi(n).

For a computed product C=A B whose operands already have errors, the first-order analysis uses err(C,n)=mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||+||A||err(B,n)+err(A,n)||B||. The surrounding text identifies err as an absolute normwise error.

The exact ordinary problem is A R-R B=-C. For upper-triangular A and B it is the triangular linear system associated with all differences A_ii-B_jj and is nonsingular precisely when A and B have distinct eigenvalues.

With conformal 2-by-2 block partitions and upper-triangular A and B, multiplication gives four exact Sylvester equations: A22 R21-R21 B11=-C21; A11 R11-R11 B11=-C11-A12 R21; A22 R22-R22 B22=-C22+R21 B12; and A11 R12-R12 B22=-C12+R11 B12-A12 R22. R21 is solved first, then R11 and R22, and finally R12.

For square n-by-n matrices with n a power of two, SylR returns -C/(A-B) when n=1. Otherwise it recursively computes R21=SylR(A22,B11,C21), R11=SylR(A11,B11,C11+A12 R21), R22=SylR(A22,B22,C22-R21 B12), and R12=SylR(A11,B22,C12-R11 B12+A12 R22), in that order.

source_evidence.anchor: paragraph and cost recurrence following SylR
source_evidence.observation: With conventional O(n^3) multiplication, SylR performs the same arithmetic operations and rounding errors as a conventional Sylvester solver, only reordered. Its cost obeys cost(n)=4 cost(n/2)+O(n^{omega+eta})=O(n^{omega+eta}) provided omega+eta>2.

source_evidence.anchor: Kronecker formulation, definition of sep, and equation (19)
source_evidence.observation: The equation is written (I tensor A-B^T tensor I)vec(R)=-vec(C), with vec stacking columns from left to right. The separation is sep(A,B)=sigma_min(I tensor A-B^T tensor I)=min_{||R||_F=1}||A R-R B||_F. Every recursive diagonal-block problem satisfies sep(A_ii,B_jj)>=sep(A,B). The induction bound err(n') includes errors in forming recursive right-hand sides.

source_evidence.anchor: four block-error inequalities, aggregate recurrence, and equation (20)
source_evidence.observation: The page gives separate first-order bounds for R21, R11, R22, and R12, sums them into an affine recurrence with coefficient 4+2(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B), and derives both displayed asymptotic bounds culminating in equation (20). It compares this with the conventional forward bound O(epsilon||R||(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B)) and concludes that SylR is logarithmically stable.

For the generalized pair A R-L B=-C and Abar R-L Bbar=-Cbar, conformal block expansion produces four generalized Sylvester subproblems, one per output subblock, which the paper says are solved consecutively and recursively as before. No generalized error recurrence is displayed.

binders: Let n be a positive power of two; A, B, C, and the solution R are square n-by-n matrices, with each recursion operating on n/2-by-n/2 blocks. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchor "power-of-two assumption"; PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "SylR pseudocode"]

A and B are upper triangular, C is conformally partitioned, and R denotes the exact solution of A R-R B=-C when exact and computed quantities are being distinguished through err. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchors "ordinary Sylvester equation" and "equation (14)"]

epsilon is machine epsilon, mu(m) is the polynomial growth factor in the stable m-by-m multiplication model, and '+eta' means any eta>0. [PDF page 2 (printed 60), anchors "equation (1)" and "for any eta>0"]
hypotheses: The spectra of A and B are disjoint, equivalently the Sylvester coefficient system is nonsingular; hence sep(A,B)>0. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchor "nonsingular precisely when the eigenvalues of A and B are distinct"; PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "definition of sep"]

Matrix products used in the analysis obey the normwise first-order stable-multiplication model inherited from (1) and (8). [PDF page 2 (printed 60), anchor "equation (1)"; PDF page 8 (printed 66), anchor "equation (8)"]

For each smaller problem, err(n') is assumed inductively to bound its solution error, including error incurred while computing its right-hand side. [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "induction hypothesis following (19)"]

Each recursive problem inherits sep(A_ii,B_jj)>=sep(A,B), so a right-hand-side perturbation of norm at most x changes its solution by at most x/sep(A,B). [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "equation (19)"; PDF page 28 (printed 86), opening sentence]
conclusions: The exact block dependencies are A22 R21-R21 B11=-C21; A11 R11-R11 B11=-C11-A12 R21; A22 R22-R22 B22=-C22+R21 B12; and A11 R12-R12 B22=-C12+R11 B12-A12 R22. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchor "equations (15)-(18)"]

SylR computes, in order, R21=SylR(A22,B11,C21), R11=SylR(A11,B11,C11+A12 R21), R22=SylR(A22,B22,C22-R21 B12), and R12=SylR(A11,B22,C12-R11 B12+A12 R22), with scalar base case R=-C/(A-B). [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "SylR pseudocode"]
The first block satisfies err(R21,n/2)<=err(n/2). [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "first block-error inequality"]

The R11 bound is err(R11,n/2)<=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C11||+||A12||err(R21,n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||A12||||R21||]/sep(A,B), and then <=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C||+||A||err(n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||A||||R||]/sep(A,B). [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "R11 error inequality"]

The R22 bound is err(R22,n/2)<=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C22||+||B12||err(R21,n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||B12||||R21||]/sep(A,B), and then <=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C||+||B||err(n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||B||||R||]/sep(A,B). [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "R22 error inequality"]

The R12 bound is err(R12,n/2)<=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C12||+||B12||err(R11,n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||B12||||R11||+||A12||err(R22,n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon||A12||||R22||]/sep(A,B), and then <=err(n/2)+[epsilon||C||+(||A||+||B||)err(n/2)+mu(n/2)epsilon(||A||+||B||)||R||]/sep(A,B). [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "R12 error inequality"]

Summing block errors gives err(R,n)<=sum_ij err(Rij,n/2)<=[4+2(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B)]err(n/2)+epsilon[3||C||+2mu(n/2)(||A||+||B||)||R||]/sep(A,B). The displayed equality for err(n) is the recurrence defining this upper bound, not an exact identity for the realized error. [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "aggregate block-error inequality and affine recurrence"]

Solving the recurrence gives err(n)<=O((n epsilon/sep(A,B))(||C||+mu(n/2)(||A||+||B||)||R||)(2+(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^{log_2 n}) and then equation (20): err(n)<=O(n^{1+log_2 3}mu(n/2)epsilon||R||((||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^{1+log_2 n}). [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "equation (20)"]

Because a conventional Sylvester solver has forward error O(epsilon||R||(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B)), the recursive algorithm is declared logarithmically stable. [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "comparison following (20)"]

The arithmetic cost is O(n^{omega+eta}) when omega+eta>2; using conventional O(n^3) multiplication reproduces the conventional solver's arithmetic and rounding errors in a different order. [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "cost recurrence following SylR"]

For the generalized equations A R-L B=-C and Abar R-L Bbar=-Cbar, the paper claims only that block expansion yields four generalized Sylvester equations solved consecutively and recursively as before. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchor "generalized Sylvester equation"; PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "generalized Sylvester sketch"]

statement.algorithm_linkage: SylR is the recursive ordinary-Sylvester solver implementing the exact dependencies (15)-(18), with a scalar division base case and the explicit order R21, R11, R22, R12. The equation-(20) analysis applies to this ordinary solver. The generalized two-equation variant is only block-expanded and said to recurse similarly; no generalized pseudocode or error bound is supplied. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchors "equations (15)-(18)" and "generalized Sylvester equation"; PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "SylR pseudocode"; PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchors "equation (20)" and "generalized Sylvester sketch"]
numerical_model: Stable matrix multiplication is modeled by ||C_comp-A B||<=mu(m)epsilon||A||||B||+O(epsilon^2), with mu(m) a low-degree polynomial. [PDF page 2 (printed 60), anchor "equation (1)"]
When operands inherit prior errors, the first-order product rule is mu(m)epsilon||A||||B||+||A||err(B,m)+err(A,m)||B||. [PDF page 8 (printed 66), anchor "equation (8)"]

The SylR derivation is explicitly first order and uses machine epsilon epsilon; products of inherited errors and other O(epsilon^2) contributions are omitted. [PDF page 8 (printed 66), anchors "first order error analysis" and "equation (8)"; PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "error inequalities"]

With conventional O(n^3) multiplication, SylR has the same arithmetic operations and rounding errors as a conventional Sylvester solver, merely reordered. [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "paragraph following SylR"]

The paper-wide precision result says matching backward-stable accuracy may require up to chi(n) times the baseline number of bits and at most a quadratic factor in chi(n) in bit complexity. [PDF page 7 (printed 65), anchor "Lemma 3.2"]
error_notions: err(R,n) is an absolute normwise forward-error bound for the computed solution, not a residual or backward-error bound. [PDF page 8 (printed 66), anchor "absolute error preceding (8)"; PDF pages 27-28 (printed 85-86), anchors "induction hypothesis" and "err(R,n)"]
Errors made while computing recursive right-hand sides are explicitly included in err(n'). [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "including errors in computing the right-hand side"]

norms: The separation sep(A,B) is explicitly defined using the Frobenius norm on R and A R-R B; equivalently it is the smallest singular value of the vectorized coefficient matrix. [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "definition of sep"]

The error inequalities and equation (20) use unsubscripted norms for A, B, C, R, and errors. Section 6.3 does not explicitly identify those unsubscripted norms. [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "four block-error inequalities and equation (20)"]

The global multiplication model is normwise and says norm changes are permitted at the expense of dimension-dependent polynomial factors. [PDF page 2 (printed 60), anchor "discussion following equation (1)"]
constants_and_indexing: The block indices are 11, 12, 21, and 22; upper triangularity removes A21 and B21, while R and C retain all four blocks. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), anchor "equation (14)"]

The dependency order is R21 first, R11 second, R22 third, and R12 last; equations (16) and (17) are both enabled by R21, although the pseudocode fixes their order as R11 then R22. [PDF page 26 (printed 84), text following (18); PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchor "SylR pseudocode"]

Equation (20) retains mu(n/2), the factor n^{1+log_2 3}, and the conditioning-ratio exponent 1+log_2 n. [PDF page 28 (printed 86), anchor "equation (20)"]

contract_plain_english: For upper-triangular n-by-n A and B with disjoint spectra, n a power of two, and n-by-n C, the exact target is the unique R satisfying A R-R B=-C. SylR obtains R by solving the four exact block equations in the fixed order R21, R11, R22, R12, ending in scalar divisions. [PDF pages 26-27 (printed 84-85), anchors "equations (15)-(18)" and "SylR pseudocode"] The conditioning quantity is sep(A,B)=min_{||X||_F=1}||A X-X B||_F, and every recursive diagonal-block problem has separation at least sep(A,B). [PDF page 27 (printed 85), anchors "definition of sep" and "equation (19)"] Under the paper's first-order normwise stable-multiplication model, the four block-error estimates sum to the stated affine recurrence and yield equation (20): O(n^{1+log_2 3}mu(n/2)epsilon||R||((||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^{1+log_2 n}). [PDF pages 2 and 28 (printed 60 and 86), anchors "equation (1)", "four block-error inequalities", and "equation (20)"] Comparing this with the conventional forward bound makes the ordinary recursive solver logarithmically stable, with O(n^{omega+eta}) arithmetic cost when omega+eta>2; the generalized equation receives only a recursive block sketch. [PDF pages 27-28 (printed 85-86), anchors "cost recurrence", "comparison following (20)", and "generalized Sylvester sketch"]
